en: The amihan wind brings cool, dry air to the Philippines from November to February, creating the ideal dry season for farmers to harvest and dry crops.
The Valley Fault System stretches across Luzon and can cause major earthquakes, which is why buildings in Metro Manila must follow strict earthquake-resistant codes.
Zambales province contains large chromite deposits, a hard mineral used to make stainless steel and protect metals from rusting.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River features an eight-kilometer underground river that flows directly into the sea, showing groundwater moving through porous limestone rock.
Mayon Volcano in Albay frequently erupts, depositing nutrient-rich volcanic ash that makes the surrounding soil highly fertile for growing abaca plants.
PAGASA names typhoons using a specific list of Filipino words, like Yolanda or Rolly, to help local communities easily remember and prepare for storms.
The Philippines launched its first microsatellite, Diwata-1, into low Earth orbit to take pictures of the country and monitor natural disasters like typhoons.
During a full moon, the gravitational pull of the moon creates higher high tides in Manila Bay, which local fishermen use to navigate their boats.
During an El Niño season, the Philippines experiences severe dry spells that lower water levels in the Angat Dam, affecting the water supply of Metro Manila.
When Taal Volcano erupts, it releases pumice, a lightweight volcanic rock full of air holes that can actually float on the water of Taal Lake.
The habagat or southwest monsoon brings heavy rains to the western Philippines, often causing floods in low-lying Manila and triggering landslides in mountainous areas.
The Banaue Rice Terraces use carefully maintained clay soil to hold water, creating stepped artificial ponds that allow rice to grow on steep mountains.
